blocks.text: **The problem.** Students stand in a line; `heights[i]` is the height of the student at position i. The line should be in non-decreasing order of height. Return **how many positions** have the wrong student — where `heights[i]` differs from the sorted line's value at i.

blocks.alt: heights 1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 3 compared position by position with the sorted line 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4. Positions 2, 4 and 5 differ, so the answer is 3.

blocks.text: Comparison sorting costs O(n log n). Two common situations do better. When the **values come from a small range** — heights up to 100, digits, letters, colours — you can **count** how many of each there are, and the counts *are* the sorted order: a counting sort, O(n + k). And when you only need to split values into **two or three groups** — evens and odds, below and above a pivot, 0s/1s/2s — a single **partition** pass with two pointers puts every value in its group in O(n), in place.
This chapter covers both: Height Checker counts, Sort Array By Parity partitions, and Maximum Gap uses buckets to find a sorted-order fact without fully sorting.
**Time O(n log n), space O(n).** Perfectly good — and the honest first answer.
2. Counting sort, compared on the fly

blocks.caption: Count each height, then read the sorted line off the counts while walking the real line.

blocks.text: **Time O(n + k), space O(k)** for heights up to k = 100. The sorted line is never built: the counts are read off one value at a time, and `h` only ever moves forward.

blocks.alt: Sort a copy: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Counting sort: O(n + k) time, O(k) space.

items: **Sort Colors** — counting (or a three-way partition) on the values 0, 1 and 2 (Arrays course).
**Relative Sort Array** — counting again, with a custom order. Previous chapter.
**Minimum swaps to sort** — a harder follow-up: count the cycles of the permutation.
